CHAPTER 21 - DETERMINANTS

Introduction

Every square matrix of numbers can be assigned a single number called its DETERMINANT. This one number carries a surprising amount of information: it tells us whether a matrix has an inverse, whether a system of linear equations has a unique solution, whether three points lie on a straight line, and what the area of a triangle is. In this chapter we learn how to write and evaluate determinants of order 2 and order 3, how to expand them along any row or column using minors and cofactors, the powerful PROPERTIES that let us simplify a determinant before evaluating it, and two important applications - finding the area of a triangle and solving systems of linear equations by Cramer's rule. Throughout, we write the determinant of a square matrix A as det(A) or |A|.

21.1 DETERMINANT OF A SQUARE MATRIX

A determinant is defined ONLY for a SQUARE matrix (equal number of rows and columns). To every square matrix A we attach a number |A|. For a matrix of order n we speak of a determinant of order n. The determinant is written by enclosing the array of numbers between two vertical bars, not brackets. Thus if
   A = [ a  b ]
       [ c  d ]
then its determinant is written
   |A| = | a  b |
         | c  d |
Note the difference: a MATRIX is an arrangement of numbers (written with square brackets), while a DETERMINANT is a single NUMBER computed from a square matrix (written with vertical bars). A determinant of order 1, that is |a|, is simply the number a itself (here the bars do NOT mean modulus).

21.2 EVALUATING A 2x2 DETERMINANT

For a second-order (2x2) determinant the value is the product of the leading (principal) diagonal minus the product of the other diagonal:
   | a  b |
   | c  d |  =  a d - b c
The diagonal from top-left to bottom-right (a, d) is the leading diagonal; the diagonal from top-right to bottom-left (b, c) is the secondary diagonal. For example,
   | 2  3 |
   | 1  4 |  =  (2)(4) - (3)(1)  =  8 - 3  =  5.
Another: | 5  -2 ; 3  1 | = (5)(1) - (-2)(3) = 5 + 6 = 11.

21.3 EVALUATING A 3x3 DETERMINANT (EXPANSION ALONG A ROW OR COLUMN)

A third-order determinant is
   | a1  b1  c1 |
   | a2  b2  c2 |
   | a3  b3  c3 |
To evaluate it we EXPAND along a row or a column. Expanding along the first row:
   |A| = a1 (b2 c3 - b3 c2) - b1 (a2 c3 - a3 c2) + c1 (a2 b3 - a3 b2).
Each element of the chosen row is multiplied by the 2x2 determinant left after deleting its own row and column, and the terms are combined with the fixed sign pattern
   + - +
   - + -
   + - +
Worked example:
   | 1  0  2 |
   | 3  1 -1 |
   | 2  4  1 |
Expanding along the first row:
   = 1 * |1 -1 ; 4 1| - 0 * |3 -1 ; 2 1| + 2 * |3 1 ; 2 4|
   = 1 * (1*1 - (-1)*4) - 0 + 2 * (3*4 - 1*2)
   = 1 * (1 + 4) + 2 * (12 - 2)
   = 5 + 20 = 25.
The value of a determinant does NOT depend on which row or column we expand along - every choice gives the same number. It is usually smart to expand along the row or column that contains the most zeros, because each zero kills a whole term.

21.4 MINORS AND COFACTORS

The MINOR of an element is the determinant obtained by deleting the row and the column in which that element lies. In a 3x3 determinant the minor of any element is a 2x2 determinant. We write the minor of the element in row i and column j as M_ij.

The COFACTOR of an element is its minor multiplied by a sign (-1)^(i+j). We write the cofactor as A_ij:
   A_ij = (-1)^(i+j) M_ij.
The sign factor (-1)^(i+j) follows the checkerboard pattern +, -, + along the first row, and so on.

Example. For
   A = | 1  2  3 |
       | 4  5  6 |
       | 7  8  9 |
the minor of the element 1 (row 1, col 1) is M_11 = |5 6 ; 8 9| = 45 - 48 = -3, and its cofactor is A_11 = (+1)(-3) = -3. The minor of 2 (row 1, col 2) is M_12 = |4 6 ; 7 9| = 36 - 42 = -6, and its cofactor is A_12 = (-1)(-6) = 6. The minor of 3 is M_13 = |4 5 ; 7 8| = 32 - 35 = -3, cofactor A_13 = (+1)(-3) = -3.

A determinant equals the sum of the products of the elements of ANY row (or column) with their OWN cofactors:
   |A| = a1 A_11 + b1 A_12 + c1 A_13   (expansion along row 1).
This is exactly the expansion of Section 21.3 written in cofactor language. A useful related fact: the sum of the products of the elements of one row with the cofactors of a DIFFERENT row is ZERO.

21.5 PROPERTIES OF DETERMINANTS

These properties let us simplify a determinant, often reducing it to a triangular form or creating zeros before expanding.

Property 1 (Transpose). The value of a determinant is unchanged if its rows and columns are interchanged: |A| = |A^T|. Hence any statement true for rows is equally true for columns.

Property 2 (Interchange of two rows/columns). If any two rows (or two columns) of a determinant are interchanged, the value of the determinant changes SIGN (is multiplied by -1).

Property 3 (Identical rows/columns). If any two rows (or two columns) of a determinant are identical (or proportional), the value of the determinant is ZERO. This follows from Property 2: swapping the two equal rows leaves the determinant unchanged yet must change its sign, so |A| = -|A|, forcing |A| = 0.

Property 4 (Scalar multiple). If every element of one row (or one column) is multiplied by a constant k, the whole determinant is multiplied by k. Read the other way, a common factor of a row or column can be TAKEN OUT in front of the determinant. As a consequence, for an n x n matrix, det(kA) = k^n det(A), because a factor k comes out of each of the n rows.

Property 5 (Sum of determinants). If each element of a row (or column) is written as a sum of two terms, the determinant can be split into the sum of two determinants.

Property 6 (Row/column operation). If to the elements of any row (or column) we add k times the corresponding elements of another row (or column), the value of the determinant is UNCHANGED. In symbols R_i -> R_i + k R_j (i not equal to j) leaves |A| unaltered. This is the most useful property for creating zeros.

Property 7 (Zero row/column). If any row or column consists entirely of zeros, the determinant is ZERO.

Property 8 (Triangular determinant). If all the elements below (or all above) the leading diagonal are zero, the determinant equals the product of the diagonal elements.

Worked example using properties: evaluate
   | 1  1  1 |
   | a  b  c |
   | a^2 b^2 c^2 |
Applying C2 -> C2 - C1 and C3 -> C3 - C1 (column operations) and taking out common factors gives (b - a)(c - a)(c - b). This is the well-known Vandermonde determinant; it is zero whenever any two of a, b, c are equal, as Property 3 predicts.

21.6 AREA OF A TRIANGLE USING DETERMINANTS

If a triangle has vertices (x1, y1), (x2, y2) and (x3, y3), its area is
   Area = (1/2) | x1 (y2 - y3) + x2 (y3 - y1) + x3 (y1 - y2) |,
which can be written compactly as the modulus of a third-order determinant:
   Area = (1/2) * abs of  | x1  y1  1 |
                          | x2  y2  1 |
                          | x3  y3  1 |
Because area is always positive we take the absolute value (modulus) of the determinant; the factor 1/2 and the modulus together give the geometric area.

Worked example: vertices (0, 0), (4, 0), (0, 3).
   Area = (1/2) | 0(0 - 3) + 4(3 - 0) + 0(0 - 0) | = (1/2) |0 + 12 + 0| = 6 square units.

CONDITION FOR COLLINEAR POINTS. Three points are COLLINEAR (lie on one straight line) exactly when the triangle they form has zero area, that is when
   | x1  y1  1 ; x2  y2  1 ; x3  y3  1 | = 0.
This determinant test is a quick way to check collinearity and to find the equation of a line through two points.

21.7 SOLVING LINEAR SYSTEMS - CRAMER'S RULE

Determinants give a neat formula for the solution of a system of linear equations, known as CRAMER'S RULE.

TWO VARIABLES. For
   a1 x + b1 y = c1
   a2 x + b2 y = c2
let
   D  = | a1  b1 ; a2  b2 |   (determinant of the coefficients),
   Dx = | c1  b1 ; c2  b2 |   (replace the x-column by the constants),
   Dy = | a1  c1 ; a2  c2 |   (replace the y-column by the constants).
If D is not zero, the unique solution is
   x = Dx / D,   y = Dy / D.
Worked example:
   2x + 3y = 8
    x +  y = 3
   D = |2 3 ; 1 1| = 2 - 3 = -1,  Dx = |8 3 ; 3 1| = 8 - 9 = -1,  Dy = |2 8 ; 1 3| = 6 - 8 = -2.
   x = Dx/D = -1/-1 = 1,  y = Dy/D = -2/-1 = 2. So x = 1, y = 2.

THREE VARIABLES. For
   a1 x + b1 y + c1 z = d1
   a2 x + b2 y + c2 z = d2
   a3 x + b3 y + c3 z = d3
let D be the 3x3 determinant of the coefficients, and let Dx, Dy, Dz be the determinants obtained by replacing the x-, y-, z-columns respectively by the column of constants d1, d2, d3. If D is not zero,
   x = Dx / D,   y = Dy / D,   z = Dz / D.
Worked example:
   x + y + z = 6
   x + 2y + 3z = 14
   x + 4y + 9z = 36
   D = |1 1 1 ; 1 2 3 ; 1 4 9| = 1(18-12) - 1(9-3) + 1(4-2) = 6 - 6 + 2 = 2.
   Dx = |6 1 1 ; 14 2 3 ; 36 4 9| = 2, Dy = |1 6 1 ; 1 14 3 ; 1 36 9| = 4, Dz = |1 1 6 ; 1 2 14 ; 1 4 36| = 6.
   x = 2/2 = 1, y = 4/2 = 2, z = 6/2 = 3.

21.8 CONSISTENCY OF A SYSTEM

A system is CONSISTENT if it has at least one solution and INCONSISTENT if it has none. Cramer's rule classifies the possibilities through the determinants:

(1) If D is not zero: the system has a UNIQUE solution (it is consistent and independent).

(2) If D = 0 and each of Dx, Dy, Dz is also zero: the system has INFINITELY MANY solutions (consistent and dependent) - provided the equations are genuinely proportional; the equations then represent the same line or plane.

(3) If D = 0 but at least one of Dx, Dy, Dz is not zero: the system has NO solution (it is inconsistent) - for example two parallel lines.

Thus the single number D = 0 is the CONDITION at which a unique solution fails; whether we then get no solution or infinitely many depends on Dx, Dy, Dz. For a HOMOGENEOUS system (all constants zero: d1 = d2 = d3 = 0), x = y = z = 0 is always a solution (the trivial one); a NON-trivial solution exists only when D = 0.

SUMMARY

- A determinant is a single number |A| attached to a SQUARE matrix; order 1 gives |a| = a.
- 2x2: |a b ; c d| = ad - bc (leading diagonal product minus secondary diagonal product).
- 3x3: expand along any row or column; |A| = a1(b2c3 - b3c2) - b1(a2c3 - a3c2) + c1(a2b3 - a3b2). The answer is the same whichever row/column is chosen; pick the one with most zeros.
- Minor M_ij = determinant left after deleting row i and column j; cofactor A_ij = (-1)^(i+j) M_ij. A determinant equals the sum of each row's (or column's) elements times their own cofactors.
- Properties: |A| = |A^T|; swapping two rows/columns changes the sign; two identical or proportional rows/columns give 0; a common factor of a row/column comes out (det(kA) = k^n det(A)); R_i -> R_i + k R_j leaves the value unchanged; a zero row/column gives 0; a triangular determinant is the product of its diagonal.
- Area of a triangle with vertices (x1,y1),(x2,y2),(x3,y3) is (1/2)|det of [x1 y1 1 ; x2 y2 1 ; x3 y3 1]|; the three points are collinear when this determinant is 0.
- Cramer's rule: x = Dx/D, y = Dy/D (and z = Dz/D) when D is not zero, where Dx, Dy, Dz replace the relevant column by the constants.
- Consistency: D not 0 gives a unique solution; D = 0 with all of Dx, Dy, Dz = 0 gives infinitely many solutions; D = 0 with some of them not 0 gives no solution.

topics.name: Determinant of a Matrix
topics.description: The determinant |A| or det(A) as a single number attached to a SQUARE matrix; the difference between a matrix (an array) and a determinant (a number); notation with vertical bars; order of a determinant and the order-1 case |a| = a.

topics.name: Evaluating 2x2 and 3x3 Determinants
topics.description: Value of a 2x2 determinant as ad - bc; expansion of a 3x3 determinant along a row or column with the +,-,+ sign pattern; the value is independent of the row/column chosen, so expanding along the line with most zeros is easiest.

topics.name: Minors and Cofactors
topics.description: The minor M_ij as the determinant left after deleting row i and column j; the cofactor A_ij = (-1)^(i+j) M_ij; expansion of a determinant as the sum of elements of a row/column times their own cofactors.

topics.name: Properties of Determinants
topics.description: Transpose invariance |A| = |A^T|; sign change on interchanging two rows/columns; zero for identical or proportional rows/columns; scalar factor of a row (det(kA) = k^n det A); invariance under R_i -> R_i + k R_j; zero row/column; triangular determinant equals the diagonal product.

topics.name: Area of a Triangle using Determinants
topics.description: Area = (1/2)|det of [x1 y1 1 ; x2 y2 1 ; x3 y3 1]| for a triangle with the given vertices; use of the modulus because area is positive; the collinearity condition that the determinant vanishes.

topics.name: Cramer's Rule and Consistency of Systems
topics.description: Solving 2- and 3-variable linear systems by x = Dx/D, y = Dy/D, z = Dz/D; the coefficient determinant D and the replaced-column determinants Dx, Dy, Dz; the consistency conditions for a unique solution, no solution and infinitely many solutions.

learning_outcomes.description: Explain what a determinant is, distinguish a determinant from a matrix, write a determinant with vertical bars, and state that a determinant is defined only for a square matrix with |a| = a for order 1.
Evaluate a 2x2 determinant using ad - bc and apply it to simple numerical and algebraic determinants.
Expand and evaluate a 3x3 determinant along any row or column using the +,-,+ sign pattern, choosing the row/column with most zeros.
Find the minor and cofactor of any element of a determinant and expand a determinant as the sum of products of elements with their cofactors.
State and use the properties of determinants (transpose, row/column interchange, identical rows, scalar multiple, row operations, zero row, triangular form) to simplify or evaluate a determinant.
Apply row and column operations and factor-extraction to prove identities and evaluate higher determinants efficiently, including det(kA) = k^n det(A).

learning_outcomes.topic_name: Area of a Triangle using Determinants
learning_outcomes.description: Compute the area of a triangle from its vertices using a determinant and test three points for collinearity using the zero-area condition.

learning_outcomes.topic_name: Cramer's Rule and Consistency of Systems
learning_outcomes.description: Solve systems of two and three linear equations by Cramer's rule and classify a system as having a unique solution, no solution or infinitely many solutions using D, Dx, Dy, Dz.

chapter_summary.title: Determinants - Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This is the NIOS Senior Secondary Mathematics (311) summary for the Determinants lesson. It explains what the determinant of a square matrix is, how to evaluate 2x2 and 3x3 determinants by expansion, minors and cofactors, the properties that simplify determinants, and two applications - the area of a triangle and solving linear systems by Cramer's rule with the conditions for consistency.

sections.heading: Meaning and evaluation of a determinant
bullets: A determinant |A| or det(A) is a single number attached to a SQUARE matrix; it is written with vertical bars, not brackets.
A 2x2 determinant equals the leading-diagonal product minus the secondary-diagonal product: |a b ; c d| = ad - bc.
A 3x3 determinant is evaluated by expanding along any row or column using the sign pattern +,-,+ on the elements.
The value is the same whichever row or column is used, so it is best to expand along the one containing the most zeros.

sections.heading: Minors and cofactors
bullets: The minor M_ij of an element is the determinant left after deleting its row and column.
The cofactor is A_ij = (-1)^(i+j) M_ij, i.e. the minor with a checkerboard sign.
A determinant equals the sum of the products of the elements of any one row (or column) with their own cofactors.
The sum of the elements of one row times the cofactors of a different row is zero.

sections.heading: Properties of determinants
bullets: Rows and columns may be interchanged without changing the value: |A| = |A^T|.
Interchanging two rows or two columns changes the sign; two identical or proportional rows/columns give 0.
A common factor of a row or column can be taken outside; for order n, det(kA) = k^n det(A).
Adding a multiple of one row/column to another (R_i -> R_i + k R_j) does not change the value; a zero row/column gives 0.

sections.heading: Area of a triangle and collinearity
bullets: Area = (1/2) times the modulus of the determinant with rows (x1,y1,1), (x2,y2,1), (x3,y3,1).
The modulus is taken because area must be positive.
Equivalently Area = (1/2)|x1(y2-y3) + x2(y3-y1) + x3(y1-y2)|.
Three points are collinear exactly when this determinant equals zero (zero area).

sections.heading: Cramer's rule and consistency
bullets: For a system, D is the coefficient determinant and Dx, Dy, Dz replace the matching column by the constants.
When D is not zero the unique solution is x = Dx/D, y = Dy/D, z = Dz/D.
D = 0 with all of Dx, Dy, Dz zero gives infinitely many solutions (consistent, dependent).
D = 0 with some of Dx, Dy, Dz non-zero gives no solution (inconsistent).

key_takeaways: A determinant is one number obtained from a square matrix; |a b ; c d| = ad - bc and 3x3 determinants are found by cofactor expansion.
Expand along the row or column with the most zeros; the answer is independent of the choice.
Minor M_ij deletes row i and column j; cofactor A_ij = (-1)^(i+j) M_ij; |A| = sum of element times its cofactor.
Key properties: |A| = |A^T|; swapping two rows/columns flips the sign; equal/proportional rows give 0; R_i -> R_i + k R_j is value-preserving; det(kA) = k^n det(A).
Area of a triangle = (1/2)|det [x1 y1 1 ; x2 y2 1 ; x3 y3 1]|, and the points are collinear when the determinant is 0.
Cramer's rule: x = Dx/D, y = Dy/D, z = Dz/D provided D is not zero.
Consistency: D not 0 => unique; D = 0 and all Dx=Dy=Dz=0 => infinitely many; D = 0 and some not 0 => no solution.

glossary.definition: A single number |A| or det(A) associated with a square matrix; written between vertical bars.
The number of rows (equal to the number of columns) of the square array; a 3x3 determinant has order 3.
The diagonal of a determinant running from the top-left element to the bottom-right element.
A second-order determinant whose value is ad - bc for the array with rows (a,b) and (c,d).
Evaluating a determinant as a signed sum of elements of a row/column times their minors or cofactors.
The determinant M_ij obtained by deleting the row and column of an element from a determinant.
The signed minor A_ij = (-1)^(i+j) M_ij of an element of a determinant.
The rule that a determinant is unchanged when its rows and columns are interchanged: |A| = |A^T|.
The step R_i -> R_i + k R_j (or on columns) that adds a multiple of one line to another without changing the value.
A determinant with all entries on one side of the leading diagonal zero; its value is the product of the diagonal entries.
Area = (1/2)|det [x1 y1 1 ; x2 y2 1 ; x3 y3 1]| for a triangle with the given vertices.
Points lying on one straight line; they satisfy the determinant condition that the triangle's area is zero.
A method giving x = Dx/D, y = Dy/D, z = Dz/D for a linear system when the coefficient determinant D is not zero.
The determinant formed from the coefficients of the variables in a linear system.
A system of equations that has at least one solution; inconsistent systems have none.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Determinants (NIOS Senior Secondary Mathematics)
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Show full working for every numerical problem. A 2x2 determinant is ad - bc; expand a 3x3 along the row or column with most zeros.

questions.question: Evaluate the determinant | 4  3 ; 2  5 |.
Evaluate | 1  2  3 ; 0  1  4 ; 5  6  0 | by expanding along the first row.
For the determinant | 1  2  3 ; 4  5  6 ; 7  8  9 |, find the cofactors A_11, A_12 and A_13 of the first row.
Using a property of determinants, show that | 1  2  3 ; 2  4  6 ; 5  1  7 | = 0 without full expansion.
questions.answer:
Look at the first two rows: R2 = (2, 4, 6) = 2 x (1, 2, 3) = 2 x R1. So R2 is proportional to R1.

By the property that a determinant with two proportional (or identical) rows is zero, the value of the determinant is 0.

questions.question:
Solve the following system by Cramer's rule:
   x + y + z = 6
   x + 2y + 3z = 14
   x + 4y + 9z = 36.
Find the area of the triangle whose vertices are (2, 3), (4, -1) and (6, 7).
Show that the points (1, 2), (2, 4) and (3, 6) are collinear using a determinant.
questions.answer:
The points are collinear if | x1 y1 1 ; x2 y2 1 ; x3 y3 1 | = 0.

   | 1 2 1 ; 2 4 1 ; 3 6 1 |
   = 1(4 - 6) - 2(2 - 3) + 1(12 - 12)
   = 1(-2) - 2(-1) + 1(0)
   = -2 + 2 + 0 = 0.

Since the determinant is 0, the three points are collinear.

questions.question: Solve by Cramer's rule: 3x + 2y = 7 and x - y = -1.
Evaluate | 1  2  3 ; 2  3  1 ; 3  1  2 | using the row operation R1 -> R1 + R2 + R3 to take out a common factor, then check by direct expansion.
questions.answer:
Add all three rows into R1 (R1 -> R1 + R2 + R3). Each column of the new R1 becomes 1+2+3 = 6, so R1 = (6, 6, 6):

   | 6 6 6 ; 2 3 1 ; 3 1 2 |.

Take the common factor 6 out of R1:

   = 6 | 1 1 1 ; 2 3 1 ; 3 1 2 |.

Expand along row 1:
   = 6 [ 1(3*2 - 1*1) - 1(2*2 - 1*3) + 1(2*1 - 3*3) ]
   = 6 [ 1(6-1) - 1(4-3) + 1(2-9) ]
   = 6 [ 5 - 1 - 7 ] = 6(-3) = -18.

Check by direct expansion of the original along row 1:
   1(3*2 - 1*1) - 2(2*2 - 1*3) + 3(2*1 - 3*3) = 1(5) - 2(1) + 3(-7) = 5 - 2 - 21 = -18. Same value.
questions.explanation: Common factor 6 out of R1; both methods give -18.

questions.question: Test whether the system x + y = 3 and 2x + 2y = 6 has a unique solution, no solution or infinitely many solutions.
questions.answer:
D = |1 1 ; 2 2| = (1)(2) - (1)(2) = 2 - 2 = 0.
Dx = |3 1 ; 6 2| = (3)(2) - (1)(6) = 6 - 6 = 0.
Dy = |1 3 ; 2 6| = (1)(6) - (3)(2) = 6 - 6 = 0.

Since D = 0 and Dx = Dy = 0, the system has INFINITELY MANY solutions (the second equation is just twice the first, so both represent the same line).
questions.explanation: D=0 with Dx=Dy=0 gives infinitely many solutions.

questions.answer: The minor M_ij of an element is the determinant obtained by deleting the row and column that contain that element. questions.question: State any three properties of determinants.
questions.answer:
(1) The value of a determinant is unchanged when rows and columns are interchanged: |A| = |A^T|.
(2) Interchanging any two rows (or columns) changes the sign of the determinant.
(3) If any two rows (or columns) are identical or proportional, the determinant is zero. (Other valid properties: a common factor of a row can be taken out; R_i -> R_i + k R_j leaves the value unchanged; a zero row gives 0.)

By the property that a determinant having two proportional (or identical) rows is zero, the value of this determinant is 0.

questions.question: Prove that | 1 1 1 ; a b c ; a^2 b^2 c^2 | = (b - a)(c - a)(c - b).
questions.answer:
Apply column operations C2 -> C2 - C1 and C3 -> C3 - C1:

   | 1 0 0 ; a (b-a) (c-a) ; a^2 (b^2 - a^2) (c^2 - a^2) |.

Expand along row 1 (only the first entry survives):

   = 1 * | (b-a) (c-a) ; (b^2 - a^2) (c^2 - a^2) |.

Take out (b - a) from column 1 and (c - a) from column 2, using b^2 - a^2 = (b-a)(b+a):

   = (b - a)(c - a) * | 1 1 ; (b+a) (c+a) |
   = (b - a)(c - a)[(c + a) - (b + a)]
   = (b - a)(c - a)(c - b).

questions.answer:

A matrix is only an ARRANGEMENT of numbers (written with square brackets) and is not itself a number, whereas the determinant is the one number obtained from it. questions.answer:
Expansion along row 1 (signs +, -, +):
   = 1 * |1 -1 ; 4 1| - 0 * |3 -1 ; 2 1| + 2 * |3 1 ; 2 4|
   = 1(1 + 4) - 0 + 2(12 - 2)
   = 5 + 20 = 25.

Verification along column 2 (elements 0, 1, 4; signs -, +, -):
   = -0 * |3 -1 ; 2 1| + 1 * |1 2 ; 2 1| - 4 * |1 2 ; 3 -1|
   = 0 + 1(1 - 4) - 4(-1 - 6)
   = (-3) - 4(-7) = -3 + 28 = 25.

Both expansions give 25, confirming that the value is independent of the row or column chosen.
questions.explanation: Row-1 and column-2 expansions both give 25.

questions.question: For the determinant | 1 2 3 ; 4 5 6 ; 7 8 9 |, find the minors and cofactors of every element of the first row, and use them to evaluate the determinant.
State the main properties of determinants used for simplification, and prove that a determinant with two identical rows is zero.
questions.answer:
Main properties:
1. |A| = |A^T| (rows and columns can be interchanged).
2. Interchanging two rows or columns changes the sign of the determinant.
3. If two rows/columns are identical or proportional, the determinant is 0.
4. Multiplying one row/column by k multiplies the determinant by k; hence det(kA) = k^n det(A).
5. Adding a multiple of one row/column to another (R_i -> R_i + k R_j) leaves the value unchanged.
6. A row or column of zeros gives 0; a triangular determinant equals the product of its diagonal.

Proof that two identical rows give 0: Let |A| be the value, and suppose two rows are identical. By property 2, interchanging these two rows changes the sign, so the new determinant is -|A|. But the two rows are identical, so interchanging them leaves the determinant physically unchanged, equal to |A|. Therefore |A| = -|A|, which gives 2|A| = 0, so |A| = 0.
questions.explanation: List of properties + swap-sign proof that equal rows give 0.

questions.question: Using row/column operations, prove that | 1 1 1 ; a b c ; a^2 b^2 c^2 | = (b - a)(c - a)(c - b).
questions.answer:
Apply C2 -> C2 - C1 and C3 -> C3 - C1:

   | 1 0 0 ; a (b - a) (c - a) ; a^2 (b^2 - a^2) (c^2 - a^2) |.

Expand along the first row (only the leading 1 contributes):

   = | (b - a) (c - a) ; (b^2 - a^2) (c^2 - a^2) |.

Since b^2 - a^2 = (b - a)(b + a) and c^2 - a^2 = (c - a)(c + a), take (b - a) out of column 1 and (c - a) out of column 2:

   = (b - a)(c - a) | 1 1 ; (b + a) (c + a) |
   = (b - a)(c - a)[(c + a) - (b + a)]
   = (b - a)(c - a)(c - b).

This is the Vandermonde result; it is zero whenever any two of a, b, c are equal, matching the identical-columns property.
questions.explanation: Column operations + factoring give the Vandermonde product.

The area of a triangle with vertices (x1,y1),(x2,y2),(x3,y3) is (1/2)|det [x1 y1 1 ; x2 y2 1 ; x3 y3 1]|. If this determinant is zero the points are collinear.
(a) Find the area of the triangle with vertices (0,0),(6,0),(0,4).
(b) Why do we take the modulus?
(c) Test whether (1,1),(2,3),(3,5) are collinear.
(d) What does zero area tell you about three points?
questions.answer:
(a) Area = (1/2)|0(0 - 4) + 6(4 - 0) + 0(0 - 0)| = (1/2)|24| = 12 square units.
(b) Because area must be positive, we take the modulus of the (possibly negative) determinant.
(c) | 1 1 1 ; 2 3 1 ; 3 5 1 | = 1(3 - 5) - 1(2 - 3) + 1(10 - 9) = -2 + 1 + 1 = 0, so the points are collinear.
(d) Zero area means the three points lie on one straight line (they are collinear).
questions.explanation: Area 12; modulus for positivity; collinear; zero area = one line.

Consider 2x + 3y = 8 and x + y = 3.
(a) Write and evaluate D.
(b) Evaluate Dx and Dy.
(c) Find x and y.

questions.answer:
(a) D = |2 3 ; 1 1| = 2 - 3 = -1.
(b) Dx = |8 3 ; 3 1| = 8 - 9 = -1; Dy = |2 8 ; 1 3| = 6 - 8 = -2.
(c) x = Dx/D = -1/-1 = 1, y = Dy/D = -2/-1 = 2.
(d) If D were zero, Cramer's rule would not apply directly; the system would have either no solution or infinitely many solutions instead of a unique one.
questions.explanation: D=-1; Dx=-1, Dy=-2; (1,2); D=0 means no unique solution.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A 3x3 determinant can be expanded along any row or column with the sign pattern +,-,+ / -,+,- / +,-,+.
Consider D = | 3 1 2 ; 2 0 -1 ; 1 4 5 |.
(a) Expand along the first row to evaluate D.
(b) Which row or column would have been easier and why?
(c) State the cofactor sign for the element in row 2, column 3.
(d) Is the answer affected by the choice of expansion line?
questions.answer:
(a) D = 3 * |0 -1 ; 4 5| - 1 * |2 -1 ; 1 5| + 2 * |2 0 ; 1 4|
     = 3(0 + 4) - 1(10 + 1) + 2(8 - 0)
     = 12 - 11 + 16 = 17.
(b) Row 2 (or column 2) contains a zero, so expanding there gives one fewer 2x2 determinant to compute.
(c) The sign for row 2, column 3 is (-1)^(2+3) = -.
(d) No. The value 17 is the same whichever row or column is used.
questions.explanation: D = 17; row/col with a zero is easier; sign -; value invariant.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A linear system is classified by its determinants: D not 0 gives a unique solution; D = 0 with all of Dx, Dy, Dz zero gives infinitely many solutions; D = 0 with some non-zero gives no solution.
(a) For x + y = 2 and x + y = 5, evaluate D and Dx and classify the system.
(b) For 2x + 3y = 5 and 4x + 6y = 10, evaluate D, Dx, Dy and classify the system.
(c) For x + y = 3 and x - y = 1, evaluate D and classify the system.
(d) What single determinant decides whether a unique solution exists?
questions.answer:
(a) D = |1 1 ; 1 1| = 0; Dx = |2 1 ; 5 1| = 2 - 5 = -3 (not zero). D = 0 with Dx not zero => NO solution (inconsistent; the lines are parallel).
(b) D = |2 3 ; 4 6| = 12 - 12 = 0; Dx = |5 3 ; 10 6| = 30 - 30 = 0; Dy = |2 5 ; 4 10| = 20 - 20 = 0. D = 0 with Dx = Dy = 0 => INFINITELY MANY solutions (same line).
(c) D = |1 1 ; 1 -1| = -1 - 1 = -2 (not zero) => UNIQUE solution.
(d) The coefficient determinant D: a unique solution exists exactly when D is not zero.
questions.explanation: No solution; infinitely many; unique; D decides uniqueness.
